lessons.title: Fumigants and the principles of fumigation
lessons.html:
What makes fumigation different

A fumigant is a pesticide that acts as a gas. It penetrates into wall voids, timber, furniture, packaging and commodities, reaching pests that sprays cannot. That same property makes fumigants extremely dangerous: the gas moves wherever air moves, cannot be contained by gloves or overalls, and can kill people quickly. Structural fumigation is therefore one of the most tightly controlled activities in pest management, and may only be carried out by operators registered for fumigation under Act 36 of 1947.

Structural fumigation situations

  • Whole buildings or rooms infested with drywood termites or wood borers.
  • Flour mills, food factories and warehouses with stored product insects in the structure and equipment.
  • Shipping containers, vessels and wooden packaging for quarantine or export requirements, such as treatment of wood packaging material under the international ISPM 15 standard where fumigation is the chosen method.
  • Churches, museums and furniture with heritage timber damage.

Common fumigants

FumigantNotes
Phosphine (from aluminium or magnesium phosphide products)Widely used; slow acting, needs adequate exposure time and temperature; corrosive to copper, silver and gold, so damages electrical and electronic equipment
Sulfuryl fluorideUsed for structural pests such as drywood termites and wood borers where registered; odourless, so no warning smell
Methyl bromideOzone-depleting; phased out under the Montreal Protocol except for limited quarantine and pre-shipment uses where still permitted

The dose principle: concentration and time

Fumigation success depends on holding a lethal gas concentration for long enough. This is often expressed as the concentration multiplied by the exposure time, the CT product. Low concentration for a long time and high concentration for a short time are not always equivalent; each fumigant and pest stage responds differently, and eggs and pupae are often most tolerant. Follow the label for dose, minimum exposure period and minimum temperature.

Factors affecting success

  • Gas-tightness: leaks are the main cause of failure and of danger to bystanders.
  • Temperature: lower temperatures slow insect metabolism and gas activity, requiring longer exposure.
  • Sorption: some materials absorb gas, lowering the concentration.
  • Wind: increases leakage through tarpaulins and gaps.

lessons.title: Planning and preparing a structural fumigation
lessons.html:
Planning is the safety system

Most fumigation accidents are failures of planning: someone left inside, a neighbour exposed by leaking gas, or re-entry before clearance. A written fumigation management plan, prepared and checked in advance, is standard good practice and is required by many labels and clients.

Contents of the fumigation management plan

  • Site description, structure, volume calculation and sealing method.
  • Pest identified and fumigant, dose, exposure time and temperature considerations, from the label.
  • Risk assessment: adjacent buildings, occupied areas, drains, basements and underground services through which gas could travel.
  • Exclusion or buffer zone and how it will be secured.
  • Notifications to occupants, neighbours and any authorities or parties as required by the label, local by-laws or the client.
  • Personnel, their roles, registration and training; respiratory protection and gas monitoring equipment.
  • Emergency procedures, nearest medical facility, first aid and the product's emergency contact.
  • Aeration and clearance procedure.

Preparing the structure

  1. Evacuate all people and animals, including pets, birds and fish. Remove plants where the label requires.
  2. Remove or protect food, feed, medicines and items that could be affected, following the label for the fumigant used.
  3. Protect or remove sensitive equipment where phosphine is used, because of corrosion of copper and precious metals.
  4. Switch off pilot lights, open flames and electrical appliances as required by the label.
  5. Open internal doors, cupboards and drawers to allow gas distribution.
  6. Seal the structure: tape gaps and vents, or tarp the whole building with gas-proof sheets weighted with sand snakes.
  7. Post warning signs on all entrances and around the perimeter, with the fumigant name, date, time, emergency contact and a skull-and-crossbones warning, in languages understood locally.
  8. Check every room, roof space and outbuilding to confirm that nobody is inside, with a second person verifying. Lock and secure all entrances.

lessons.title: Conducting, monitoring and clearing the fumigation
lessons.html:
Releasing the fumigant

Fumigant is introduced according to the label method, ideally from outside the structure. Where entry is needed, at least two trained persons work together with respiratory protection as the label specifies, and one remains outside as standby. Never work alone with fumigants.

Monitoring during exposure

  • Measure gas concentrations inside the structure at planned points using suitable monitors or sampling lines, to confirm that the target concentration is reached and maintained.
  • Monitor the perimeter and nearby occupied areas for leaks. If gas is detected outside the exclusion zone, stop the source if possible, extend the zone, warn people and repair the leak.
  • Secure the site for the full exposure period with guarding or regular patrols as the risk requires.
  • Record readings, times, temperatures, weather and actions taken.

Aeration

After the exposure period, the structure is ventilated to remove the gas. Open the structure from outside where possible, starting on the downwind side, using fans as planned. Maintain the exclusion zone during aeration because outflowing gas is concentrated.

Clearance

  1. Test the air throughout the structure, including enclosed spaces and furnishings, with an instrument suited to the fumigant.
  2. Clearance is given only when concentrations are below the re-entry level specified by the label and applicable occupational exposure requirements.
  3. Remove and correctly deactivate or dispose of fumigant residues according to the label. Phosphide residues can still release gas and must never be placed in closed bins or water without following the label procedure.
  4. Issue a written clearance certificate to the client, stating date and time of clearance and readings.
  5. Remove warning signs only after clearance.

Emergencies

Signs of phosphine exposure can include headache, dizziness, nausea, chest tightness and breathing difficulty. Do not enter a gassed area to rescue anyone without appropriate breathing apparatus and a standby person. Move the casualty to fresh air, call emergency services and take the label. First aid must follow the label and SDS, and fumigation teams need hands-on first aid training from an accredited provider.

Key points

  • Structural fumigation may only be done by operators registered for fumigation under Act 36 of 1947.
  • Success depends on gas concentration held for enough time, gas-tightness and temperature.
  • A written fumigation management plan covers risks, exclusion zones, notifications, roles and emergencies.
  • Confirm that no person or animal remains inside before release, and never work alone.
  • Clear only when tested concentrations are below the label re-entry level, then issue a clearance certificate.
